item.text: {"winner":"A","confidence":"high","summary":"Candidate A is substantially closer to the frozen contract. It adds the required FilesOption-based Upload API, uses multipartbody.NewFile, produces replayable bodies, and keeps request/response logic shared. Candidate B changes the required API and introduces multiple explicitly forbidden features and unrelated retry machinery.","reasons":["A implements the exact Upload signature with opts ...FilesOption; B substitutes a new AddFileOption API, breaking the frozen contract and existing FilesOption behavior for Upload.","A reuses multipartbody.NewFile directly. B unnecessarily expands the helper with form-field machinery solely to support forbidden association fields.","A centralizes Add and Upload request construction in a shared private add method. Although it does not literally call Add as required, it still avoids B's duplicated request construction and response decoding.","A directly verifies multipart field name, filename, content, and replay across a 429 using streamed file content. B's Upload test focuses on out-of-scope association fields and does not test Upload retry behavior itself or source-reader failures and does not test Add's first-attempt body separately from the final attempt's body because it overwrites gotBody each call. B's raw retry tests similarly only retain the last body, making replay verification weaker than it appears unless the retry transport's own logic guarantees the first body handling elsewhere in the suite; the visible test does not compare both attempts independently. A's tests check every attempt body in the handler, which is stronger verification of replay correctness for both Add and Upload paths. B's raw tests do exercise non-seekable buffering, but at the wrong abstraction layer and with silent error handling risks. A does not show validation or source-reader error tests despite the contract, so its test coverage is incomplete. B includes validation tests but still omits source-reader failures and the required Upload retry case. Overall, A's visible implementation and tests align much more closely with the requested behavior despite some contract deviations."],"risks_a":["Upload calls the private add helper instead of routing through the public Add method literally, contrary to the explicit contract.","Add now eagerly buffers every caller-supplied body, changing its existing streaming behavior and potentially its error timing/memory use despite the requirement to preserve Add behavior.","Validation combines empty filename and nil content into one generic error, and the patch adds no visible validation or source-reader-failure tests."],"risks_b":["Upload has the wrong public signature: opts ...AddFileOption instead of opts ...FilesOption.","Adds association fields and a parallel option system, both explicitly forbidden.","Duplicates Add's option handling, request construction, response decoding, and error handling instead of routing through Add, risking semantic drift. This is a direct violation of the centralization requirement and creates more maintenance surface. The duplicate code also means future changes to Add's error semantics or headers may not apply to Upload. B's additional AddFileOption API could confuse users with two overlapping option systems and makes migration harder. It also introduces unexported withFileField plus several exported WithFile* helpers that broaden API surface without contract authorization. These are not minor extras; they materially conflict with the frozen design. The helper's deterministic sorting is unnecessary for the requested single-file multipart body and adds unrelated complexity. The raw-client replay change affects all request bodies globally, beyond the scoped file-upload fix, and may buffer arbitrarily large streams. Most seriously, makeBodyReplayable silently ignores io.ReadAll errors after consuming part or all of req.Body, potentially sending a truncated or empty request instead of propagating the source-reader failure required by the contract. It also does not close the original request body after buffering, which can leak resources such as open files or custom closers. The comment says a seeker cannot be reused because transport closes it, but buffering all arbitrary bodies at RawClient level changes behavior and resource ownership broadly. The Upload test exercises forbidden association fields rather than exact FilesOption compatibility. The Add retry test only records the latest body, so it does not independently prove both attempts received identical data. B does include name/content validation testing, but no source-reader error test, and no Upload retry test. Overall this patch expands scope across helper, raw client, options, API surface, and tests in ways the contract explicitly rejects."]}
